Excellencies, dear colleagues, it is our great pleasure to present today the interim report of the Joint Working Group established to consider the recommendations contained in the Joint Inspection Unit review of the governance and oversight of the executive boards of UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS, UNICEF, and UN Women of 2023. The GIU review identified 10 formal and 21 informal recommendations in 6 thematic areas: roles and responsibilities, board composition and structure, secretariat functions, meeting practices, oversight and advisory committees, and risk management. At the Annual Session 2024, the Executive Boards established the Joint Working Group we are presenting today and tasked it with reviewing all 31 recommendations and develop actionable implementation pathways. The Working Group's terms of reference were formally adopted at the first Regular Session of last It is important to emphasize that the Working Group advises and the Executive Board, of course, decides. On the work undertaken to date, since its establishment, the Working Group has conducted a detailed assessment of all recommendations, developed a roadmap and working methods, consulted with the 5 organizations who participate in this exercise, issued questionnaires to gather updated information, and engaged regularly with member states through briefings and updates at each formal session. The proposals contained in the report you have before you reflect the working group's assessment of all the recommendations, identifying those proposed for acceptance, partial acceptance, non-acceptance, or considered completed. Some words on the guiding principle. Throughout its work, the Joint Working Group has been guided by the overarching principle of strengthening and optimizing existing mechanisms of the Executive Boards wherever possible before proposing the creation of new structures. This approach is deliberately aligned with the objectives of the UN Haiti Initiative, which calls for lean, efficient, and effective governance across the UN system. Thank you, Annette. Thank you, Mr. Chair. On key findings, among the key proposals of the working group is the development of a comprehensive harmonized informal guidance document a delegate's handbook to be jointly drafted by the secretariats of all 5 organizations. The handbook would be consolidated— would consolidate the roles, responsibilities, and procedures of executive board members covering governance, oversight, risk management, and secretariat arrangements. It would address the substance of several related recommendations. And can be updated as needed. It avoids duplication. The draft would be submitted to the executive boards for consideration, allowing for structured discussions and further refinements as needed. A key gap identified by the JIU concerns the reporting line between internal audit and oversight committees and the executive boards. The working group proposes updating existing charters and terms of reference to establish a direct reporting line to the executive boards in addition to the executive heads, including simultaneous transmission of annual reports and post-meeting summaries, aimed to explicitly codify the principle of unrestricted access of oversight, oversight functions to the boards. The working group considers this will further strengthen the alignment and independence of Audits and Oversight Committees. On the recommendation related to the establishment of appropriate board committees, the working group acknowledges that current arrangements are generally adequate but recognizes that the volume and technical complexity of documentation combined with limited session time may constrain the depth of board deliberations, particularly on oversight and finance. The Working Group proposes to explore the possible establishment of a standing advisory committee covering audit, risk, budget, and finance, composed of a limited number of member state experts with equitable geographical representation. Further consideration, including its mandate, reporting arrangements, and interaction with boards, would take place in a context of the working method review. Ensuring complementarity with existing oversight bodies and preserving the primacy of the board and decision-making. On review of working methods, the working group proposes a dedicated review of the working methods of the executive boards of the participating organizations, followed, followed by periodic assessment at agreed intervals. The review would address the harmonization of work plans, the relationship between informal and formal meetings, the quality and clarity of board decisions, and the inclusiveness of member state participation. It would also provide the appropriate context for further consideration of possible advisory subcommittee, as mentioned above. The Working Group proposes a formal consultation mechanism requiring executive directors to notify boards in writing with rationale prior to the appointment, renewal, or termination of heads of independent oversight functions should be reflected in the updated Charter and Terms of Reference. The Working Group proposes that the Secretariats jointly develop harmonized Terms of Reference clarifying roles, reporting lines, impartiality, and accountability, complemented by annual informal consultations between Bureau and Secretariat heads to ensure resource adequacy is regularly reviewed. Moving on to the overview of proposed positions. Of the 31 recommendations, the working group proposed to accept 15 in full, partially accept 7, not accept 7, and consider 2 as completed. Recommendations proposed for non-acceptance generally relate to matters considered adequately addressed through existing arrangements. Or recommendations that have already been completed after the, the review or reports of the JIU, where the working group judges that intervention would add procedural complexity without commensurate benefits. The working group invites the executive boards to decide on one of three models for guiding implementation. Continuation of the Joint Working Group in its current revised form, establishment of new standing committee on institutional governance, or direct oversight of implementation by executive boards themselves. Thank you, Ambassador, distinguished members of the Executive Board. It is a pleasure to be here today as we present you the new UNDP Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2029. My remarks will focus on the 2025 Annual Report on the strategy and then on the new strategy. The Annual Report points out to three clear conclusions: First, UNDP consistently delivers its commitments and continues to achieve strong results through its country programmes. Second, our institutional performance remains solid, meeting or exceeding 83% of the rigorous UN SWAP 3.0 new requirements. Third, UNDP continues to invest at scale, with 75% of expenditure contributing to gender equality. The results are reflected in concrete gains. From 2022 to 2025, 155 million women gained access to financial services and 182 million to basic services. 177 public institutions and 330,000 civil servants advance reforms that improve public policy and service delivery for all people. The strategy, the new strategy, was developed through an unprecedented broad consultation involving more than 3,500 participants, 152 UNDP country offices, and a wide range of external partners, with two messages as a result. First, There is a strong expectation that UNDP helps countries place gender equality at the core of their decisions. Second, there is a clear recognition of UNDP's implementation capacity, at scale, in our areas of strength. What is different in this Strategy is that gender equality is not treated as a sectoral priority. But as a systemic accelerator of development, embedded in the economic, political and environmental structures that determine people's lives. In response, the new Strategy focuses more directly on the roots of inequality and concentrates UNDP's efforts where we bring clear value added: social protection and care, fiscal policy, elections, public institution reform, environmental action, recovery and peacebuilding. It also gives great attention to emerging challenges, including technology-facilitated violence and the risk that digital and AI transitions reinforce existing inequalities. This is about future-proofing development. The qualitative leap of this strategy is that it connects what is too often treated separately, such as budget, care system, environmental policy, so countries can serve their populations, all of their populations, better. Partnerships are central to us. For instance, our partnership with UN Women is a core element of this strategy and reflects the direction of UNAID: a more effective and coordinated UN system. Finally, The Strategy also recognizes that our progress is built through internal transformation. Our impact on gender equality depends on the strength of our own internal policies, structures, cultures and ways of working. Over the next 4 years, we will achieve this through: more integrated actions across portfolios and teams; an internal culture grounded in respect and dignity; and more diverse financing models to translate commitment into delivery. Distinguished Member States and our Administrator said gender equality is not a single-side agenda. It is how development becomes more effective and more sustainable. We are grateful for all the engagement that helped develop this Strategy. We look forward to working with all Member States and partners to translate this ambition into results. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair.

It is incumbent on the UN to keep a sharp focus on transitioning all efforts to national actors, guided by the receiving government and financed by national public and private sector resources. While we note that these country programs are mapped against national development frameworks that are linked to the Sustainable Development Goals, the United States reiterates that we consider the SDGs to be a soft form of global governance. We will not recognize them as a matter of course. Regarding the further extension of the South Sudan Country Program, the United States is deeply concerned that UNDP's work is entrenching international aid dependency by perpetuating an unsustainable, unsustainable status quo that harms the South Sudanese people. The CDP— I'm sorry, the CPD portrays South Sudan as making institutional progress despite clear evidence to the contrary. Claims of improved fiscal discipline and public financial management contradict the transitional government's systematic corruption, general institutional collapse, and failure to pay salaries for almost 2 years. Proposed support to tax administration, budgeting, and revenue mobilization ignore the chronic budget non-compliance, entrenched corruption, and opaque oil revenue management issues that the CPD itself identifies. UNDP proposals to support electoral institutions, transitional justice mechanisms, national and subnational legislative bodies, health systems, private sector-led development, and large-scale environmental initiatives are simply divorced from the realities on the ground in South Sudan. Rule of law programming risks reinforcing abusive institutions. Health plans ignore a total absence of national cofinancing in a donor-substituted sector. The CPD's ambitions for diversification Private sector development and improved planning far exceed what ministries characterized by extreme turnover, no funding, and limited capacity can absorb. We expect all CPDs to be clear-eyed about risk, time-bound, and consider donor concerns. Thank you.
